newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Lower Russian sales restrict platinum supply.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Lower Russian sales restrict platinum supply.

text.p: World supplies of platinum are forecast to fall 140,000 ounces to 4.85 million ounces in 1996 due to lower Russian exports, Johnson Matthey's Platinum 1996 Interim Review reported on Tuesday.
Lower supply from Russia will be partially offset by an additional 40,000 ounces coming out of South Africa despite mine production there being hit by labour problems.
Russia is forecast to ship about 1.10 million ounces of platinum, down 180,000 ounces from 1995, according to the report.
World demand for the metal is seen down about 30,000 ounces to to 4.77 million ounces.

"But that is a bit misleading in that most of the decline has come from a fall (of 110,000 ounces down to 235,000 ounces) in demand for large investment bars in Japan which is a very volatile sector," said the report's author Alison Cowley.
"The main underlying demand trend from consumers is basically up due to higher industrial demand, a slight rise in jewellery demand and more going to China," she added.
The report saw platinum prices ranging between $370 and $400 an ounce in the next six months. On Tuesday it fixed at $388.25.
Johnson Matthey (JM) is the world's largest refiner of the platinum group metals which also include palladium and rhodium.

Platinum is used in jewellery, autocatalysts to clean poisonous gases from car exhaust, a wide variety of industrial applications and as an investment vehicle almost exclusively in Japan, the largest user of the metal.
Worldwide, industrial use of the metal is forecast to rise by seven percent from 1995 to a 17-year high of 1.065 ounces.
Use of platinum for jewellery should reach a new high this year of 1.84 million ounces, up 30,000 ounces, as demand rises in the United States, Asia and Europe.

But use for autocatalysts, which grew annually until 1993, was forecast to shrink by about 30,000 ounces to 1.82 million ounces as car manufacturers in Europe, Japan and the United States use more of the less expensive palladium-rich catalysts.
However, platinum demand will rise in the developing automotive markets of Asia and Latin America and more will be used on diesel-engined cars in Europe.
Cowley said that although Russian exports of platinum were likely to decline this year, sales would exceed 1996 production levels as they had done routinely in recent years.
"They are selling between 400,000 and 500,000 ounces from reserves - about half their shipment this year," said Cowley.

Keith Green, marketing director of JM's precious metals marketing division, said: "We believe (Russia's) production has remained at least at last year's levels so exports are down on a reduction in their sales from reserves."
Most of the export decline was in lower shipments to Japan, which JM said had imported 28 percent less platinum from Russia in the first seven months of this year compared with 1995.
"The overall Japanese imports of platinum are down slightly but only a matter of three-four percent. This year the Japanese are taking more metal from South Africa," Cowley said.

Japan consumed 2.22 million ounces of the metal last year out of total world consumption of 4.80 million ounces. It will use a forecast 2.03 million ounces in 1996 from world figures of an estimated 4.77 million.
The JM report forecast China would import about 180,000 ounces of platinum this year compared with 130,000 ounces in 1995 as the country upgrades its industrial base.
"It also used 100,000 ounces for platinum jewellery which is more platinum jewellery than was consumed in the United States," Green said.
